extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, and journalists interested in Hong Kong media and Apple Daily
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing evaluative criteria, practices, and metrics used to describe a single newspaper (Apple Daily) — its format, editorial stance, content style, circulation, legal/ethical history, digital presence, and vulnerability to political pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Modelled after USA Today: printing in full colour and concise writing; broadsheet format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper was modelled after USA Today, with printing in full colour and concise writing; it used large colourful graphics. These presentation choices positioned it as a mass-market broadsheet with tabloid-style visual emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and register
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensively used written Cantonese when most Hong Kong newspapers used written vernacular Chinese.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apple Daily's use of written Cantonese made its prose distinctive and accessible to Cantonese-speaking readers; this linguistic choice is cited as a notable editorial/content decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content focus / beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on reporting crime, celebrity news, eroticism, gambling, and drug use; strong entertainment coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At launch it carried at least three pages of entertainment news (later increased to eight by 2000). The newspaper emphasised crime and celebrity scandal coverage as core beats, which contributed to its high circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabloid journalism / sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduced tabloid journalism to Hong Kong; emphasis on sensationalist stories such as celebrity scandals, traffic accidents and deaths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as introducing tabloid journalism to Hong Kong, Apple Daily used sensationalist headlines and large visuals. Scholar commentary links this approach to transforming broadsheet newspapers into tabloids and to replication by competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial position / political alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit editorial stance described as pro‑democracy, anti‑government, or anti‑China; vocal support for pro‑democracy movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper's editorial position (pro‑democracy and critical of the Hong Kong/Chinese governments) affected advertising, political pressure, and made it a target for authorities; it also informed campaigns encouraging civic participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking news and investigative exclusives
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong coverage of breaking news and current affairs; produced exclusive reports on political scandals (e.g., Cheng Kai‑nam, Antony Leung).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apple Daily was known for breaking-news coverage, live-streaming events (e.g., raids), and publishing exclusives and investigative pieces that exposed political scandals—factors that enhanced its news-value and public profile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation and digital reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Measured by print circulation and online unique visitors: e.g., print circulation ~86,000 (2021), website ~9.6 million monthly unique visitors; final issue printed over one million copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulation and digital metrics are used to quantify reach and influence; spikes (e.g., final-issue 1 million copies, surge in online traffic) also indicate public support or response to events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and ethical breaches (defamation, source payments, bribery)
rubrics_metrics.description: History of legal/ethical problems: court-ordered damages for defamation; reporter jailed for bribing police; paid sources to pose for photographs and later apologised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific incidents (HK$3.6 million defamation judgment, reporter sentencing for bribing police, paying a bereaved man for a photo) illustrate risks to credibility and legal compliance; they serve as negative indicators in evaluating journalistic ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self‑regulation and industry compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Did not join the self‑regulation panel of the Newspaper Society of Hong Kong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-participation in industry self-regulation is presented as a notable institutional choice and may bear on external accountability and complaints-handling practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial leadership and staffing
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial leadership (editors‑in‑chief roster, first female chief editor in 2015) and arrests of senior staff affected the paper's operations and direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in editorship and the arrest/ detention of senior executives are cited as shaping editorial policy, staff morale, and the paper's ability to operate; leadership profiles are used to evaluate institutional stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader engagement and activism
rubrics_metrics.description: Used social media campaigns and public mobilisation (e.g., encouraging readers to buy copies, donate or buy stock) to rally support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaigns (print-buying, stock purchases, livestreaming production) demonstrate methods of sustaining readership and signaling public support—relevant when assessing influence and community ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability to political and legal pressure (press freedom risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject to police raids, arrests under the national security law, asset freezes and eventual closure; these events are framed as attacks on press freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper's experience—raids, live-streamed searches, frozen assets, arrests—serves as criteria for assessing an outlet's exposure to state repression and operational sustainability under political pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy issues, partisan misinformation and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Published a factually inaccurate 64-page report alleging Hunter Biden ties; ran opinion pieces supporting Donald Trump and promoting falsehoods; led to resignations and apologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances of publishing contested or false material and partisan campaigning are cited as harms to credibility; downstream consequences (resignations, apologies, reputational damage) are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cybersecurity and external attack resilience
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated denial‑of‑service attacks described as professional cyberattacks that may have been coordinated by the Chinese government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention of FireEye's assessment positions cybersecurity as an operational quality criterion—frequency and sophistication of attacks indicate risk environment and technical resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business strategy and pricing tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaged in aggressive pricing and promotional tactics (e.g., initial coupons reducing cover price, T-shirts, posters) that helped boost early circulation amid a price war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of promotional pricing and marketing campaigns is documented as a growth strategy; the resulting market disruption (competitor price cuts, closures of some papers) is cited as impact evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards, recognition and credibility markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Winner of journalism prizes (e.g., Hong Kong Human Rights Press Awards) and ranked in trust/use surveys (Chinese University of Hong Kong survey; Reuters Institute poll).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards and independent survey rankings are used as positive indicators of journalistic quality and public trust despite controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multilingual and multimedia presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Launched an English-language online edition (2020); operated YouTube channels and live-streamed newsroom/production activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversification into English and multimedia platforms is treated as a measure of audience reach, adaptation to digital media, and cross-lingual/technical capability.
